newsitem.title: USA: Blue chips close lower; market ignores inflation news.
newsitem.headline: Blue chips close lower; market ignores inflation news.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Wednesday after news that inflation was still in check in January failed to ignite another record-setting rally.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended 47.33 points lower at 7,020.13, one day after racing to an all-time high of 7,067.46.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,283 to 1,269 on active volume of 519 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Meanwhile, the market showed little response to news in midafternoon trading of the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.

"I think in the West, Deng was largely viewed as a figurehead, so I wouldn't expect much reaction," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co. "It's really been several years since he faded to the background and the power there has already been passed on to others."

U.S.-listed shares in China-related funds also showed little reaction to the news. Templeton China World Fund Inc. dipped 1/4 to 12-7/8 and Jardine Fleming China Region Fund Inc. was unchanged at 11-5/8.
Analysts said Wall Street was taking some profits amid disappointment that the latest good news on inflation did not spark a rally.
"This looked like a reversal of what we saw yesterday," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "People are going to view this as profit-taking."

He said a lackluster performance in the bond market despite news that the consumer price index, one of the key measures of inflation, rose only 0.1 percent last month -- its smallest monthly gain since last summer -- likely served as a catalyst for the sell-off in stocks.
The increase followed a 0.3 percent rise in December.
"I think the bond market's failure to respond to that news was part of the problem," he said. "It certainly might have been the excuse to take some profits in stocks."

The bond market also fell, with the 30-year Treasury bond off 13/32, or $4.06 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.58 percent from 6.55 percent Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Technology shares generally outperformed the broader market, helped by Hewlett-Packard Co.'s strong quarterly earnings, which were released late Tuesday. Hewlett-Packard rose 2-3/16 to 54-3/8.
The shares of high-end computer makers were also higher, including Compaq Computer Corp., which rose 1-7/8 to 85-3/8, and Sun Microsystems Inc., up 15/16 to 34-11/16.
Financial stocks were generally weak after their torrid run since the start of the year. First Union Corp. slipped 3-1/8 to 92-1/2 and Bank of New York Co. Inc. fell 1-3/8 to 39-3/4.
In individual issues, Fluor Corp. tumbled 13-1/8 to 61-7/8 after the engineering and construction firm reported weaker than expected quarterly earnings.
First Patriot Bankshares Inc. rose 1-1/2 to 16-1/4 after agreeing to be bought by United Bankshares Inc., whose stock ended unchanged at 33-1/2.
The Nasdaq Composite index was off 0.21 of a point at 1,365.58.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 3.82 to 812.47. The American Stock Exchange index was up 1.05 at 599.15.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.50 to 425.57. The average share was down 16 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,773.109, down 19.464, or 0.25 percent.
